They point out, correctly, that the hospital and the university and the very idea that the weak have worth the strong must honor grew in soil Christendom tilled. A culture does not float free of its founding convictions, and when you pull the root you should not be surprised when the fruit rots. When such people grieve the end of Christendom, they are grieving something real. A scaffolding is coming down, and scaffolding holds things up.

So here is the answer to the strong version, not the weak one. Yes, Christendom built hospitals and a moral grammar the secular world still borrows without paying. But the same arrangement that built those things also built something the gospel never asked for, a Christianity you could inherit without ever meeting Christ. When faith is the default, faith is cheap. The end of Christendom is the end of cheap Christianity, the end of the cultural Christian who held the surname without the cross, and that is not only a loss. It is a clarification.

## The mustard seed, not the empire

The text I want to carry through this is older than the problem. The kingdom of God, Jesus said, is like a mustard seed, the smallest of seeds, which becomes a tree where the birds nest (paraphrase of Matthew 13 and following). Notice what the parable does not promise. It does not promise that the tree will own the field, or pass the laws, or seat the king. It promises growth from smallness, life from something you could lose in the dirt. Jesus described his movement in terms of the smallest thing in the garden, not the largest thing in the empire. We spent sixteen centuries assuming he meant the empire anyway.

Lesslie Newbigin saw this with unusual clarity, because he saw it from both directions. He spent decades as a missionary in India, where the church had never been the establishment, had never held cultural power, had always been a small and often suspect minority. Then he came home to England and found that the West had become a mission field too, a post-Christian society in which the church could no longer assume the culture's agreement and had to learn, all over again, how to be a witness rather than a chaplaincy. Newbigin argued that the church in the West had been so long the establishment that it had forgotten how to be the church, had confused the maintenance of a Christian society with the proclamation of the gospel, and that the collapse of Christendom was, of all things, an opportunity, a recovery of the church's actual nature as a sign and foretaste of a kingdom it does not control.

## The grief we have to examine

Here is the part I have to say to my own grief, and to my tribe's. Much of what we are grieving when we grieve the end of Christendom is not the gospel at all. It is the power. It is the loss of the default, the loss of the assumption that the culture is on our side, the loss of a comfort the early church never had and never asked for. We are grieving the catacombs in reverse, mourning the loss of the throne the wilderness told us to refuse.

And there is a specifically dangerous form this grief takes, which is the temptation to seize by force what we are losing by attrition. When a church feels its cultural power slipping, the offer on the mountain comes back, recycled one more time. Take the kingdoms. Bend the state. Use the levers while you still can. Make them respect you, since they will no longer love you. This is Christian nationalism in its most sympathetic guise, the dying establishment grasping for the throne it is losing, and it is the exact opposite of what the moment requires.

Because the church does not actually need the throne. It never did. It grew fastest when it had none. The faith that grew under Pliny's executions, afflicted but not crushed, did not need the empire's favor and was arguably purer without it. The end of Christendom is frightening only to a church that has confused the gospel with its cultural position, that cannot imagine being faithful without being powerful, that has forgotten it began as a mustard seed and not a tree that owned the field.

I have felt the grief. I have stood in the wreckage of the old arrangement and mourned, and some of the mourning was holy and some of it was idolatry, and learning to tell the two apart is most of the work in front of us. The death of Christendom is a mercy disguised as a loss. It is stripping away the cheap version, the inherited version, the version fused with the flag, and leaving the church with the only thing it ever actually had, a crucified Lord and a hope the empire could not touch.

## The faith that grew without the throne

It helps to remember that the most explosive growth in the history of the church happened before Christendom existed and is happening now, again, in places where Christendom never came. The faith that spread through the Roman world in the first three centuries had no establishment, no favorable law, no cultural default, and it grew anyway, person to person, household to household, on the strength of a witness the empire could not stop and a hope the empire could not touch. And in our own moment the church is growing fastest not in the old Christendom heartlands of the West but in places like sub-Saharan Africa and parts of Asia, often under pressure, often without power, often as a minority. The correlation between the church's cultural power and the church's actual vitality is not positive. If anything it runs the other way. The church has most often been weakest in soul when it was strongest in the world.

This should reframe the grief entirely. If the gospel grows best without the throne, then losing the throne is not losing the gospel. It may be recovering it. The end of Christendom strips away the cultural Christian, the inherited believer, the person whose faith was a surname rather than a cross, and what is left is the church that actually chose Christ, which is smaller and poorer and less powerful and, quite possibly, far more alive than the establishment ever was.

## Naming my own grief honestly

I have to be honest about my own grief one more time, because it is the kind of grief that hides its real object. When I mourn the world I grew up in, the world where the culture at least pretended to share my faith, I tell myself I am mourning lost souls. Sometimes I am. But often I am mourning lost comfort, lost respectability, lost ease, the world where being a Christian cost me nothing because everyone around me was nominally one too. That is not holy grief. That is the grief of a man losing a privilege, and dressing it in the language of evangelism so he does not have to call it what it is.

The hard discipline of this moment is learning to tell those two griefs apart, the holy grief for souls and the idolatrous grief for power, because they feel identical from the inside and lead in opposite directions. The holy grief sends the church back to witness, to the patient, costly, person-to-person work the early church did without any establishment behind it. The idolatrous grief sends the church to the mountain, to the offer of the kingdoms, to the temptation to seize by force the cultural power it is losing by attrition. Same tears. Opposite roads. And the church that cannot tell them apart will keep mistaking a grab for power for a passion for the gospel.

Christendom is ending. Let it. Christianity is not, and it never depended on Christendom, and the church that finally understands the difference will be free in a way the church of power never was.
chapters.verdict: What is dying is not the faith. It is the comfort of never having to choose it.
reflect: You grieve the end of Christendom. How much of that grief is for the gospel, and how much is for the power, the comfort, and the cultural default the early church never had and never asked for?

Newbigin called the collapse of Christendom an opportunity to recover the church's actual nature. What would change in your church if it stopped trying to maintain a Christian society and started living as a mustard seed it does not control?

When cultural power slips away by attrition, the temptation is to seize it by force. Where do you feel the pull to make the culture respect you since it will no longer love you, and how is that the wilderness offer recycled?

chapters.title: The Cost of a Free Church
chapters.summary: A free church is not a church that has escaped politics but one that has refused to give any earthly power the worship that belongs to God alone, and the freedom costs the one thing the captive church most wants to keep.
chapters.body:
I want to end where the book began, on the mountain, with the offer still standing. Because the offer never stops standing. As long as there is a church and there are kingdoms of this world, the tempter will keep pointing at the kingdoms and saying take them, all of them, on my terms, with one small adjustment of your worship. The free church is not the church that was never offered the kingdoms. It is the church that keeps saying no.

And I should say clearly what a free church is not, because the word is easy to abuse. A free church is not a church that has retreated from public life and called the retreat holiness. It is not the privatized faith that hands Caesar the whole world and keeps God in the private heart. We have already named that as a surrender, not a freedom. The free church speaks, engages, works for justice, names the sins of the nation in the gate the way the prophets did. A church with nothing to say to Pharaoh is not free. It is absent.

The free church is the church that does all of that without giving any earthly power the worship, the trust, the ultimate hope that belong to God alone. It engages without fusing. It works for justice without confusing the legislation with the kingdom. It loves its country without worshiping it, votes without baptizing the vote, holds its convictions with all the force the gospel gives them and still keeps the seam visible between its Lord and its tribe, so that when the two diverge it can follow the Lord. That visible seam is the whole of its freedom. The captive church has lost the seam. The free church guards it with its life.

## What it costs

This freedom is expensive, and I will not pretend otherwise, because the cheap version is most of what has gone wrong.

It costs you your tribe's approval. The free church will be called a traitor by both sides, because it will indict both sides, and a tribe does not forgive the prophet who turns the blade homeward. When you apply one standard and your tribe wants two, you become useless to the tribe, and the tribe will tell you so. The free church is lonely in exactly the way the true prophets were lonely, condemned by the home crowd for refusing to flatter it.

It costs you the shortcut. The free church refuses the offer on the mountain, which means it refuses to reach the kingdom's ends by the world's means, which means it gives up the speed and the force and the worldly effectiveness that the captive church enjoys. It is slower. It looks weaker. It loses elections it could have won by selling the seam. The free church is the church that took the long road through Gethsemane when the short road over the mountain was right there, and it pays the price of the long road every single day.

And it costs you the comfort of certainty about your own side. The free church has to run the consistency check on itself first, forever, which means it never gets to rest in the clean conviction that its tribe is righteous and the other tribe is damned. It has to keep finding the high place in its own house, keep naming the second lord it added without noticing, keep being indicted by the one Word it claims to serve. That is exhausting in a way that tribal certainty never is. Tribal certainty is restful. Freedom is vigilance.

## Why it is worth the cost

But here is what the free church gets that the captive church can never have. It gets the actual gospel, undiluted, unfused, the crucified Lord who needs no flag under him because every flag flies under him. It gets a hope the empire cannot touch and an election cannot deliver and a cultural collapse cannot remove, because its hope was never in the kingdoms it was offered on the mountain. It gets to be afflicted but not crushed, struck down but not destroyed, because the thing it lives for was never the thing the world could take away.

And it gets to be a witness. The watching world, the skeptic most of all, can smell the fusion. He knows when a church has become a chaplaincy for a political army, and it is one of the chief reasons he will not come near the cross. But a church that loves its country and will still stand against it, that holds its convictions and still indicts its own side, that engages the public square and still refuses to worship it, that church is saying something the world has no other way to hear. It is saying there is a Lord above every Caesar, a kingdom above every nation, a hope above every tribe. It is saying Jesus is Lord, and meaning the treason the early church meant by it.

## The weight I leave you with

I have been captive. I want to say that plainly at the end, because this whole book has been an indictment, and the prophet who is not inside the indictment is a fraud. I grew up in the fusion. I have wanted the mountain. I have run the double standard, excused my tribe, baptized my politics, kept high places I swore were not high places, softened the one Word into a chaplain for loyalties I had already decided to keep. I am not writing from the free church. I am writing toward it, from inside the captivity, with the offer still standing in front of me on the mountain every day of my life.

The wilderness is not behind us. It is the room we live in. The kingdoms are still on the table, and the price is still a single bent knee, and the church is still saying yes far more often than it says no. The free church is not a place we arrive. It is a refusal we make again every morning, the same refusal Jesus made in the desert, the no that founds everything.

## What it looks like on a Tuesday

I do not want to leave this in the realm of grand declarations, because the free church is not built by declarations. It is built by small, ordinary, costly choices made in rooms where no one is watching. It looks like a pastor declining to turn his pulpit into a voter guide even when the donors want it and the crowd would cheer. It looks like a congregation that can pray for a president it did not vote for without irony or gritted teeth. It looks like a believer who catches himself excusing his own side and stops, and names the excuse, and applies the standard he would use on the other tribe. It looks like a family that loves its country at the parade and still teaches its children that the country is not God. It looks like an old man taking the flag off the platform, not as an insult to the dead but as an honor to the Lord, and bearing the anger that follows without bitterness.

None of that makes the news. All of it is the free church being built, one refused shortcut at a time, one named high place at a time, one consistency check at a time, in the long, slow, unglamorous work of keeping the seam visible between the cross and everything that wants to climb onto it.

## The weight I leave you with

I have been captive. I want to say that plainly at the end, because this whole book has been an indictment, and the prophet who is not inside the indictment is a fraud. I grew up in the fusion. I have wanted the mountain. I have run the double standard, excused my tribe, baptized my politics, kept high places I swore were not high places, softened the one Word into a chaplain for loyalties I had already decided to keep. I am not writing from the free church. I am writing toward it, from inside the captivity, with the offer still standing in front of me on the mountain every day of my life.

The wilderness is not behind us. It is the room we live in. The kingdoms are still on the table, and the price is still a single bent knee, and the church is still saying yes far more often than it says no.

He could have had the world that afternoon. He chose the cross. He chose it for us and as our pattern, and he handed us the same choice, the kingdoms or the cross, the flag or the Lord, the shortcut or the long road through Gethsemane.

This is not a book about politics. It is a book about who the church belongs to. And the church will not be free until it can say, with the early martyrs and the Barmen remnant and the crucified Lord himself, that Jesus is Lord and Caesar is not, that every flag flies under the cross or it has stolen a throne, that the kingdoms of this world are not worth a single bent knee.

The offer is still standing. So is the cross. Choose.
chapters.verdict: Freedom costs you your tribe. Captivity costs you your Lord.
reflect: A free church is called a traitor by both sides because it indicts both sides. Are you willing to be useless to your tribe, and if not, what does that unwillingness say about whether your church is free?

The free church runs the consistency check on itself forever and never gets to rest in the certainty that its side is righteous. Are you more drawn to the restfulness of tribal certainty or the vigilance of freedom, and why?

The author ends inside the captivity, not outside it, with the offer still standing. The kingdoms or the cross, the flag or the Lord, the shortcut or the long road: which are you actually choosing, this morning, in the rooms no one sees?
